title: Erdős Problem #85: Minimum Degree for 4-Cycles
description: Is the minimum degree threshold f(n) for forcing a 4-cycle monotone? That is, is f(n+1) ≥ f(n) for all large n?

meta.author: Erdős

meta.assumptions: 0 axioms, 0 sorries. The file states the problem (defs C4, containsC4, minDegreeForC4, Erdos85Question/Negation, starGraph, ramseyConnection, WeakerConjecture) and proves 7 axiom-free foundational lemmas about C4/containsC4/starGraph. The asymptotics f(n)=(1+o(1))sqrt(n), the Ramsey reformulation, and the monotonicity question require extremal graph theory beyond current Mathlib and remain described in doc-comments only, NOT formalized. The formalized lemmas are: the four C4 edges and a C4 non-edge, containsC4_mono (monotone under adding edges), and starGraph_not_containsC4 (stars are C4-free). Session 2 adds 4 more axiom-free structural lemmas (theoremCount 7->11, still 0 axioms/0 sorries): C4_not_adj_one_three (the second diagonal non-edge, pinning C4 to exactly its four cycle edges), containsC4_C4 (C4 contains itself via the identity embedding, so containsC4 is non-vacuous), containsC4_four_le_card (a host graph carrying a C4 has at least 4 vertices, via the injection Fin 4 -> V — the necessary size condition), and completeGraph_containsC4 (complete graphs on >=4 vertices always contain a C4, via Fin.castLE embedding + top_adj — the dense extremal counterpart to starGraph_not_containsC4). A later session adds 2 more axiom-free lemmas (theoremCount 11->13): eq_top_of_minDegree_ge (minimum degree >= n-1 on Fin n forces the complete graph, via a neighbourhood-cardinality argument with Finset.eq_of_subset_of_card_le) and minDegreeForC4_le_sub_one (the honest upper bound f(n) <= n-1 for n >= 4, chaining eq_top_of_minDegree_ge with completeGraph_containsC4; it also certifies the threshold set is non-empty so minDegreeForC4's sInf is a genuine minimum, not sInf empty = 0). A further session adds 3 more axiom-free lower-bound lemmas (theoremCount 13->16): one_le_starGraph_minDegree (the star K_{1,n} has minimum degree >= 1, no isolated vertex), two_le_minDegreeForC4 (f(n+1) >= 2 for n >= 3, since the C4-free star of min-degree >= 1 rules out any threshold <= 1 — in particular f(4) >= 2), and three_le_minDegreeForC4_five (f(5) >= 3: the 5-cycle C5 = cycleGraph 5 is 2-regular yet C4-free, verified by kernel `decide` with maxRecDepth 100000, so no threshold <= 2 forces a C4 on 5 vertices — a cycle strictly beating the star bound). The f(5) >= 3 proof uses ordinary kernel `decide`, NOT native_decide, so it remains axiom-free (propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound only, no Lean.ofReduceBool). A subsequent session (2026-07-21) adds 3 more axiom-free lemmas (theoremCount 16->19, still 0 axioms/0 sorries): cycleGraph_not_containsC4 (the n-cycle Cn is C4-free for ALL n >= 5, proved structurally without decide via the telescoping +/-1-step argument in the additive group Fin n: the four consecutive differences are +/-1 and sum to 0; injectivity of the two diagonals forces all interior steps to share one sign, so the closing difference is +/-3, contradicting +/-1 since 2 != 0 and 4 != 0 in Fin n for n >= 5 — the argument genuinely needs n >= 5 because cycleGraph 4 IS a C4), two_le_cycleGraph_minDegree (Cn is 2-regular for n >= 3), and three_le_minDegreeForC4 (the GENERAL lower bound f(n) >= 3 for every n >= 5, generalising the single-point C5 witness three_le_minDegreeForC4_five to the whole range). All three depend only on propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound (no native_decide, no Lean.ofReduceBool). A subsequent session (2026-07-21) adds 5 more axiom-free lemmas (theoremCount 19->24, still 0 axioms/0 sorries) that give the FIRST TWO exact values of the threshold and sharpen the upper bound: containsC4_of_rim (four pairwise-distinct vertices carrying the rim edges a-b, b-c, c-d, d-a host a C4, via the injective embedding ![a,b,c,d] : Fin 4 -> V — the diagonals are irrelevant), containsC4_of_minDegree_ge (minimum degree n-2 on Fin n forces a C4 for n >= 4: either G = top, or G has a non-adjacent pair a,c whose only possible non-neighbours are each other, so all n-2 >= 2 other vertices are common neighbours of both — pick two as b,d for the 4-cycle a-b-c-d-a), minDegreeForC4_le_sub_two (the sharpened upper bound f(n) <= n-2 for n >= 4, improving the crude f(n) <= n-1), and minDegreeForC4_four (f(4) = 2 EXACTLY, combining the star lower bound f(4) >= 2 with the n=4 case of the n-2 upper bound — the first exactly-determined value of f), and minDegreeForC4_five (f(5) = 3 EXACTLY, where the cycle lower bound three_le_minDegreeForC4 meets the n-2 upper bound at n=5 since 5-2=3 — the second determined value). All five depend only on propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound (host-verified with lake env lean, Lean v4.31.0). A subsequent session (2026-07-22) adds 6 more axiom-free theorems (theoremCount -> 39 public (+ 3 private helpers), lineCount 886 -> 1014, still 0 axioms / 0 sorries / no native_decide) built on a PARITY REFINEMENT of the cherry count: exists_succ_le_degree_of_odd (parity boost: on an odd number of vertices with all degrees >= an odd k, some vertex has degree >= k+1, since otherwise the degree sum is the odd number |V|*k, contradicting the handshake identity sum deg = 2|E|), minDegreeForC4_le_of_choose_lt_odd (parity-refined Kovari-Sos-Turan bound: for odd n and odd k, C(n,2) < (n-1)*C(k,2) + C(k+1,2) forces f(n) <= k — the boosted vertex upgrades the naive n*C(k,2) cherry count), minDegreeForC4_seven (f(7) = 3 EXACTLY, the FOURTH exact value: C(7,2) = 21 < 24 = 6*C(3,2) + C(4,2); both earlier upper bounds fail at n = 7 — the linear bound gives 5 and the plain cherry count only 4 since 7*C(3,2) = 21 = C(7,2) holds with equality — so it is the handshake parity that pins the value, with NO ex(7;C4) edge-bound input needed; the exact-value table is now complete for 1 <= n <= 7: f = 1,2,3,2,3,3,3), choose_lt_family (private arithmetic core: with n = 4m^2+2m+1 and k = 2m+1, n-1 = k(k-1) exactly and the doubled inequality reduces to 4m^2+2m < 4m^2+6m+2), minDegreeForC4_le_of_upper_beatty (the infinite family f(4m^2+2m+1) <= 2m+1 for every m: writing s = 2m these are the points n = s^2+s+1, the first point of the upper Beatty half-interval (s^2+s, (s+1)^2) for each even s, where the plain counting bound is provably inapplicable below sqrt(n)+2 since n > s(s+1) = k(k-1)), and minDegreeForC4_le_sqrt_add_one_of_upper_beatty (the same family bound in sqrt form: f(n) <= sqrt(n)+1 at n = 4m^2+2m+1 for m >= 1, beating the general sqrt(n)+2 bound at infinitely many points of the upper Beatty half, which no plain-counting argument reaches). All six depend only on propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound (kernel decide on small numerals only; host-verified with lake env lean, Lean v4.31.0). Three further sessions (2026-07-22) push the exact-value table from f(7) to f(10) (theoremCount 39 -> 65 public+private, lineCount 1014 -> 2168, still 0 axioms/0 sorries): f(8)=3 via a 3-regular-case reduction plus a local triangle-partition argument (3 does not divide 8); f(9)=3 via a pigeonhole common-neighbour engine that overturns a previously recorded ex(9;C4)-table blocker; and f(10)=4 via the explicit edge-list Petersen graph, with C4-freeness reduced to a 10x10 common-neighbour kernel check (not the previously blocked 10^4-embedding decide). All axiom-free.

overview.historicalContext:
This problem concerns the extremal theory of even cycles in graphs. The 4-cycle (C₄) is the simplest even cycle and appears throughout graph theory, including the Kővári–Sós–Turán theorem and the Zarankiewicz problem.

Let f(n) be the smallest integer such that every n-vertex graph with minimum degree at least f(n) contains a 4-cycle. It is known that f(n) = (1 + o(1))√n asymptotically.

Erdős asked whether f is eventually monotone: does f(n+1) ≥ f(n) hold for all sufficiently large n? This subtle question remains open. Adding vertices to a graph might create 'room' for high minimum-degree configurations that avoid 4-cycles.
overview.problemStatement:
**Erdős Problem #85 (OPEN)**

Let $f(n)$ be the minimum degree threshold such that every $n$-vertex graph with minimum degree $\geq f(n)$ contains a 4-cycle.

**Question**: Is $f(n+1) \geq f(n)$ for all sufficiently large $n$?

**Known Results**:
- $f(n) = (1 + o(1))\sqrt{n}$ asymptotically
- $f(n) < \sqrt{n} + 1$ for $n \geq 4$
- $f(4) = 2$
- Connected to Ramsey number $R(C_4, K_{1,n})$
overview.text: Is the minimum degree threshold f(n) for forcing a 4-cycle monotone? That is, is f(n+1) ≥ f(n) for all large n?
overview.proofStrategy: Defines the 4-cycle C4 on Fin 4, the containsC4 subgraph-embedding predicate, the degree-threshold function minDegreeForC4, the monotonicity question, the star graph, and the Ramsey/weaker reformulations. Adds 7 axiom-free foundational lemmas: C4_adj_zero_one/one_two/two_three/three_zero (the four cycle edges), C4_not_adj_zero_two (a diagonal non-edge), containsC4_mono (a C4 copy survives adding edges), and starGraph_not_containsC4 (the star K_{1,n} contains no C4, since its two disjoint cycle-edges would force two distinct cycle-vertices onto the centre, contradicting injectivity). A subsequent session adds the two extremal-degree lemmas eq_top_of_minDegree_ge (min-degree ≥ n−1 forces the complete graph) and minDegreeForC4_le_sub_one (the honest upper bound f(n) ≤ n−1 for n ≥ 4, which also shows the sInf defining f(n) is over a non-empty set and hence attained). The asymptotics, base case, and Ramsey connection appear in documentation only, not formalized.
keyInsights: **Minimum degree forces structure**: High minimum degree in a graph forces certain subgraphs to appear. The threshold for C₄ is well-understood asymptotically.
**Monotonicity is subtle**: Adding vertices might create room for new C₄-avoiding configurations with high minimum degree.
**Asymptotic behavior**: f(n) = (1 + o(1))√n means the threshold grows like the square root of the number of vertices.
**Ramsey connection**: The problem is intimately connected to the Ramsey number R(C₄, K_{1,n}), linking degree thresholds to Ramsey theory.
**Weaker conjecture**: A weaker form asks if f can only decrease by a bounded constant, allowing f(m) > f(n) - c for some fixed c.

**Honest ceiling and a well-defined f(n)**: An elementary axiom-free bound proves f(n) ≤ n−1 for n ≥ 4 — minimum degree n−1 on n vertices forces the complete graph, which contains a C₄. Crude next to the true (1+o(1))√n, but it certifies the threshold set is non-empty, so f(n) is a genuine minimum rather than the junk value sInf ∅ = 0. Stars K_{1,n} (C₄-free) and complete graphs (always C₄-carrying) bracket the extremal range.

**A cycle beats the star (f(5) ≥ 3)**: The generic star witness only gives f(n+1) ≥ 2, but a better C₄-free graph sharpens the lower bound. The 2-regular 5-cycle C₅ is C₄-free (verified by kernel `decide`, keeping the proof axiom-free), so no minimum-degree-2 graph on 5 vertices is forced to contain a C₄ — giving f(5) ≥ 3, just above √5 ≈ 2.24 as f(n) = (1+o(1))√n predicts. Optimal lower bounds on f(n) come from the densest C₄-free graphs, not from stars.

**Beyond counting/parity — the exact-value table now reaches f(10)**: f(8) = 3 needed a genuinely local argument (a 3-regular C₄-free graph on 8 vertices would partition into unique triangles, impossible since 3 ∤ 8) once both the cherry count and the odd-order parity boost fell silent. f(9) = 3 overturned a recorded blocker via a pigeonhole common-neighbour engine, with no extremal-table input. f(10) = 4 is the Petersen threshold: the unique (3,5)-Moore graph gives the C₄-free witness, and reducing C₄-freeness to a 10×10 common-neighbour matrix sidesteps a previously blocked 10⁴-embedding search entirely.

**From a point witness to a uniform bound (f(n) ≥ 3 for all n ≥ 5)**: The f(5) ≥ 3 witness was a finite `decide` check on ℤ/5; it generalises to *every* n ≥ 5 by a structural argument. A C₄ inside Cₙ forces four consecutive ±1 steps in the additive group Fin n that telescope to 0, while injectivity of the two diagonals locks all interior steps to the same sign — so the closing step is ±3, contradicting the ±1 an edge demands, and 2 = 0 or 4 = 0 is impossible once n ≥ 5. Thus every n-cycle is 2-regular yet C₄-free, and no threshold ≤ 2 forces a C₄, giving f(n) ≥ 3 uniformly. This replaces a case check with a proof that scales, exposing exactly why n = 4 is special (C₄ itself).

sections.title: Foundational Lemmas (axiom-free)
sections.summary: The machine-checked, axiom-free lemmas (`propext`/`Classical.choice`/`Quot.sound` only) about the concrete structures — the asymptotics, base case, and Ramsey/monotonicity questions stay documented above. C4 pinned exactly: the four cycle edges `C4_adj_zero_one/one_two/two_three/three_zero` and both diagonal non-edges `C4_not_adj_zero_two`/`C4_not_adj_one_three`. `containsC4_C4` (identity embedding, so the predicate is non-vacuous), `containsC4_four_le_card` (a host of a C₄ has ≥ 4 vertices), `containsC4_mono` (a C₄ copy survives adding edges), and the two extremal endpoints `starGraph_not_containsC4` (sparse: stars K_{1,n} are C₄-free — two disjoint cycle-edges cannot both meet the centre) and `completeGraph_containsC4` (dense: ⊤ on ≥ 4 vertices always carries a C₄, via `Fin.castLE`). Finally `eq_top_of_minDegree_ge` (min-degree ≥ n−1 on `Fin n` forces the complete graph, by a neighbourhood cardinality/`Finset.eq_of_subset_of_card_le` argument) yields `minDegreeForC4_le_sub_one`: the honest upper bound f(n) ≤ n−1 for n ≥ 4, which also certifies that the threshold set defining `minDegreeForC4` is non-empty (so its `sInf` is a genuine minimum, not the junk value `sInf ∅ = 0`).
sections.mathContext: Extremal endpoints of the C₄-forcing question: stars $K_{1,n}$ are the sparse C₄-free extreme, complete graphs $\top$ the dense C₄-carrying extreme. The honest ceiling $f(n) \le n-1$ (for $n \ge 4$) follows from `minDegree` $\ge n-1 \Rightarrow G = \top \Rightarrow C_4 \subseteq G$; it is far above the true $f(n) = (1+o(1))\sqrt{n}$ (which needs Kővári–Sós–Turán), but crucially witnesses that the defining threshold set is non-empty so $f(n) = \inf\{\dots\}$ is attained.

sections.title: Degenerate Small Cases: f(n) = n for 1 ≤ n ≤ 3 (axiom-free)
sections.summary: `minDegreeForC4_eq_self_of_le_three`: for 1 ≤ n ≤ 3 no graph on Fin n has enough vertices to carry a C₄ at all (`not_containsC4_of_card_lt_four`), so the defining threshold set holds only vacuously; the largest attainable minimum degree on Fin n is n − 1 (realised by ⊤, never exceeded), so the least k no graph reaches is k = n. This pins the boundary values f(1) = 1, f(2) = 2, f(3) = 3 — not evidence about the √n growth, which begins genuinely at n ≥ 4. Depends only on propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound.
sections.mathContext: For $n \le 3$, `containsC4` is unsatisfiable on `Fin n` (it needs an injection $\mathrm{Fin}\,4 \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Fin}\,n$), so the threshold-defining set $\{k : \forall G,\ \delta(G)\ge k \Rightarrow C_4 \subseteq G\}$ contains exactly $\{n, n+1, \ldots\}$ (since $\delta(G) \le n-1$ always), giving $f(n) = n$.

sections.title: Degree Lower Bounds and the Cycle Witness f(5) ≥ 3 (axiom-free)
sections.summary: Three axiom-free lower-bound lemmas that bracket f(n) from below using explicit C₄-free witnesses. `one_le_starGraph_minDegree`: the star K_{1,n} on Fin (n+1) has minimum degree ≥ 1 (no isolated vertex — the centre meets every leaf and each leaf meets the centre). `two_le_minDegreeForC4` (n ≥ 3): f(n+1) ≥ 2, since the C₄-free star of min-degree ≥ 1 shows no threshold ≤ 1 can force a C₄; in particular this pins the lower half f(4) ≥ 2. `three_le_minDegreeForC4_five`: f(5) ≥ 3 — the 5-cycle C₅ = `cycleGraph 5` is 2-regular yet C₄-free (a 4-cycle would need four consecutive ±1 steps in ℤ/5 summing to 0, forcing two vertices to coincide — discharged by kernel `decide` with maxRecDepth 100000, aided by the `DecidableRel C4.Adj` instance defined here), so no threshold ≤ 2 forces a C₄ on 5 vertices. This cycle witness strictly improves the generic star bound f(5) ≥ 2, and sits just above √5 ≈ 2.24 as the true asymptotic f(n) = (1+o(1))√n predicts. All three use ordinary kernel `decide`, not native_decide, so the file stays axiom-free.
sections.mathContext: Lower bounds from C₄-free witnesses: the star $K_{1,n}$ gives $f(n+1) \ge 2$ (so $f(4) \ge 2$), and the 2-regular 5-cycle $C_5$ — $C_4$-free by `decide` — gives $f(5) \ge 3 > \sqrt 5 \approx 2.24$, a cycle beating the star.

sections.title: The General Cycle Lower Bound: f(n) ≥ 3 for all n ≥ 5 (axiom-free)
sections.summary: Lifts the single-point witness f(5) ≥ 3 to a uniform bound f(n) ≥ 3 for every n ≥ 5, replacing the kernel-`decide` check on ℤ/5 with a structural ±1-step telescoping argument valid for all n. `cycleGraph_not_containsC4` (n ≥ 5): the n-cycle Cₙ is C₄-free. A copy of C₄ in `cycleGraph n` is an injection f : Fin 4 ↪ Fin n whose four consecutive images are cycle-adjacent, so each consecutive difference f(i+1) − f(i) is ±1 in the additive group Fin n. The four differences telescope to 0; injectivity of the two diagonals f₂ − f₀ and f₃ − f₁ forces all three interior steps to share the same sign, so the closing difference equals ±3 — but the closing edge also forces ±1, giving 2 = 0 or 4 = 0 in Fin n, impossible once n ≥ 5. (At n = 4 the argument genuinely fails, because `cycleGraph 4` *is* a C₄.) The proof runs inside `open Fin.CommRing in` with a `NeZero (m+2)` instance so that `ring`/`linear_combination` operate in the commutative ring Fin n. `two_le_cycleGraph_minDegree` (n ≥ 3): every vertex of Cₙ has exactly two neighbours (v−1 and v+1), so its minimum degree is 2. `three_le_minDegreeForC4` (n ≥ 5): combining the two, no threshold k ≤ 2 can force a C₄ on n vertices, hence minDegreeForC4 n ≥ 3. This uniformly improves the generic star bound f(n) ≥ 2 across all n ≥ 5 and generalises the single-point witness `three_le_minDegreeForC4_five`. The true asymptotic f(n) = (1+o(1))√n grows without bound, but that requires Kővári–Sós–Turán, beyond current Mathlib. All three theorems are axiom-free (no `decide`/`native_decide`), relying only on `linear_combination`, `omega`, and `ring` in Fin n.
sections.mathContext: From a point witness to a uniform bound: a $C_4$ inside $C_n$ forces four consecutive $\pm 1$ steps in $\mathbb{Z}/n$ that telescope to $0$, while diagonal injectivity locks their signs so the closing step is $\pm 3 \ne \pm 1$ — a contradiction once $n \ge 5$. Hence $C_n$ is $2$-regular yet $C_4$-free, giving $f(n) \ge 3$ for all $n \ge 5$, generalising the $\mathbb{Z}/5$ `decide` witness.

sections.title: Exact Threshold Values f(4)=2, f(5)=3 and the Sharpened Upper Bound f(n) ≤ n−2 (axiom-free)
sections.summary: The first exactly-determined values of the threshold function, via a sharpened upper bound. containsC4_of_rim: four pairwise-distinct vertices carrying the rim edges a-b, b-c, c-d, d-a host a C₄ through the injective embedding ![a,b,c,d] : Fin 4 → V (the diagonals are irrelevant); extracted as a standalone helper so its fin_cases case-bash runs in a minimal context. containsC4_of_minDegree_ge (n ≥ 4): minimum degree n-2 forces a C₄ — either G = ⊤ (completeGraph_containsC4), or G has a non-adjacent distinct pair a,c; since δ ≥ n-2 each vertex has ≤1 non-neighbour, so a and c can only miss each other, making every one of the n-2 ≥ 2 other vertices a common neighbour of both — pick two as b,d for the cycle a-b-c-d-a. minDegreeForC4_le_sub_two (n ≥ 4): f(n) ≤ n-2, sharpening the crude complete-graph bound f(n) ≤ n-1. minDegreeForC4_four: f(4) = 2 exactly (star lower bound f(4) ≥ 2 meets the n=4 upper bound). minDegreeForC4_five: f(5) = 3 exactly (the cycle lower bound f(5) ≥ 3 meets the n=5 upper bound, since 5-2=3). These are the first two pinned values of f; all five lemmas depend only on propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound.
sections.mathContext: A non-adjacent pair in a graph of minimum degree $n-2$ has $\ge n-2$ common neighbours, so on $\ge 4$ vertices it spans a $C_4$; hence $f(n) \le n-2$. Meeting the lower bounds $f(4) \ge 2$ and $f(5) \ge 3$ pins $f(4) = 2$ and $f(5) = 3$ — the first exact values of the minimum-degree $C_4$-threshold.

sections.title: The Kővári–Sós–Turán Counting Bound and the Third Exact Value f(6) = 3 (axiom-free)
sections.summary: The linear bounds above (f(n) ≤ n−2) are far from the truth f(n) = (1+o(1))√n; the real mechanism is the cherry double-count of Kővári–Sós–Turán. containsC4_of_card_choose_two_lt: if the number of cherries ∑_v C(deg v, 2) (paths x–v–y, counted by centre v and unordered endpoint pair {x,y}) exceeds the number C(|V|, 2) of available endpoint pairs, the pigeonhole forces two distinct cherries to share an endpoint pair — a pair {x,y} with two common neighbours v ≠ v', i.e. a 4-cycle x–v–y–v'–x. This is the z(n; 2, 2) case of KST at its simplest. minDegreeForC4_le_of_choose_lt: packaging the count as a threshold bound — whenever C(n, 2) < n · C(k, 2), every n-vertex graph of minimum degree ≥ k already contains a C₄, so f(n) ≤ k. minDegreeForC4_six: the third pinned value f(6) = 3, obtained by feeding the n=6, k=3 instance C(6,2)=15 < 6·C(3,2)=18 into the counting bound (a kernel `decide` on the choose inequality) to meet the 6-cycle lower bound f(6) ≥ 3. Depends only on propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound.
sections.mathContext: A vertex of degree $d$ is the centre of $\binom{d}{2}$ cherries $x\text{–}v\text{–}y$, and each cherry is determined by its centre and its unordered endpoint pair $\{x,y\}$. If $\sum_v \binom{\deg v}{2} > \binom{|V|}{2}$ then two cherries collide on a pair, giving two common neighbours and thus a $C_4$. Hence $\binom{n}{2} < n\binom{k}{2} \Rightarrow f(n) \le k$; at $n=6, k=3$ this reads $15 < 18$, pinning $f(6) = 3$.

sections.title: An Explicit O(√n) Upper Bound: f(n) ≤ √n + 2 (axiom-free)
sections.summary: Unfolding the implicit counting bound into a clean closed form of the correct order. Two arithmetic helpers (m·(m−1) is always even, and 2·C(m,2) = m·(m−1) — the halving in Nat.choose 2 is exact) let choose_two_lt_of_le_mul_pred turn the hypothesis n ≤ k(k−1) into the choose inequality C(n,2) < n·C(k,2) needed by the counting bound; minDegreeForC4_le_of_le_mul_pred repackages this as: n ≤ k(k−1) forces f(n) ≤ k. minDegreeForC4_le_sqrt then takes k = ⌊√n⌋ + 2, checks n ≤ k(k−1), and concludes the quotable bound f(n) ≤ √n + 2 for every n ≥ 1. This matches the true order — f(n) = (1+o(1))√n, so the leading constant 1 is sharp and only an additive O(1) is lost relative to the exact KST constant (1+√(4n−3))/2 — and dwarfs the elementary linear bound f(n) ≤ n−2. Depends only on propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound.
sections.mathContext: Taking $k = \lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor + 2$ gives $k(k-1) \ge n$, so the counting bound yields $f(n) \le \lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor + 2 \le \sqrt n + 2$ for all $n \ge 1$. The true asymptotics are $f(n) = (1+o(1))\sqrt n$ with sharp Kővári–Sós–Turán constant $\tfrac{1+\sqrt{4n-3}}{2}$; the closed form here recovers the correct leading term, losing only an additive $O(1)$.

sections.title: Sharpening the Additive Constant: f(n) ≤ √n + 1 on the Lower Beatty Half and f(m²) ≤ m + 1 (axiom-free)
sections.summary: The +2 additive constant of minDegreeForC4_le_sqrt is one worse than the sharp Kővári–Sós–Turán value k₀(n) = least k with k(k−1) ≥ n. Writing s = ⌊√n⌋, the counting bound minDegreeForC4_le_of_le_mul_pred already fires with k = s+1 exactly when k(k−1) = s(s+1) ≥ n, i.e. on the lower half s² ≤ n ≤ s²+s of each gap [s², (s+1)²). minDegreeForC4_le_sqrt_add_one packages this: whenever n ≤ √n·(√n+1) it yields the sharp f(n) ≤ √n + 1, improving the general bound by one on the lower Beatty half (on the upper half s²+s < n < (s+1)² the choice k = s+1 fails and √n + 2 is the best this argument gives). minDegreeForC4_le_sq specializes to perfect squares: since √(m²) = m and m² ≤ m(m+1), every square satisfies f(m²) ≤ m + 1 — the cleanest quotable correct-order upper bound, one better than √n + 2 and within a single additive unit of the true f(n) = (1+o(1))√n. Depends only on propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound.
sections.mathContext: With $s = \lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$, choosing $k = s+1$ in the counting bound requires $k(k-1) = s(s+1) \ge n$, which holds on the lower half $s^2 \le n \le s^2 + s$ of each interval $[s^2, (s+1)^2)$; there $f(n) \le \sqrt n + 1$, matching the sharp constant. Every perfect square $n = m^2$ lies on this lower half since $m^2 \le m(m+1)$, so $f(m^2) \le m + 1$ — one better than the general $\sqrt n + 2$ and within a single additive unit of the true $f(n) = (1+o(1))\sqrt n$.

sections.title: The Upper Beatty Half Family and the Fourth Exact Value f(7) = 3 (axiom-free)
sections.summary: A parity refinement of the counting bound. `exists_succ_le_degree_of_odd`: on an odd number of vertices with every degree ≥ an odd k, some vertex has degree ≥ k+1 (else the degree sum is the odd number |V|·k, contradicting the handshake identity). `minDegreeForC4_le_of_choose_lt_odd`: for odd n, k with C(n,2) < (n−1)·C(k,2) + C(k+1,2), the boosted vertex forces f(n) ≤ k. `minDegreeForC4_seven`: the fourth exact value f(7) = 3 — a point where BOTH earlier upper bounds fail (n−2 = 5; plain counting only gives 4 since 7·C(3,2) = 21 = C(7,2) holds with equality), so it is the handshake parity that pins the value, with no ex(7;C₄) table input needed. `choose_lt_family` (private arithmetic core) feeds an infinite family `minDegreeForC4_le_of_upper_beatty`: f(4m²+2m+1) ≤ 2m+1 for every m, and its √n form `minDegreeForC4_le_sqrt_add_one_of_upper_beatty`: f(n) ≤ √n+1 at these points, beating the general √n+2 bound on infinitely many points of the upper Beatty half (s²+s, (s+1)²) with s = 2m — a range the plain counting bound cannot reach. All axiom-free.
sections.mathContext: Handshake parity: if all degrees on an odd $|V|$ are $\ge$ an odd $k$ but none exceeds $k$, the degree sum is the odd number $|V|\cdot k$, contradicting $\sum_v \deg v = 2|E|$ (even). This upgrades the cherry count at $n=k=7$: $6\cdot\binom{3}{2}+\binom{4}{2}=24 > 21=\binom{7}{2}$, pinning $f(7)=3$. The family $n=4m^2+2m+1$, $k=2m+1$ satisfies $n-1=k(k-1)$ exactly, giving $f(n)\le\sqrt n+1$ on the upper Beatty half where plain counting is provably inapplicable.

sections.title: Beyond Counting/Parity: f(8) = 3 via the 3-Regular Case (axiom-free)
sections.summary: Cherry counting stalls at f(8) ≤ 4 (C(8,2) = 28 ≥ 24 = 8·C(3,2), no strict excess) and the odd-order parity boost is silent (8 is even). `minDegreeForC4_eight`: f(8) = 3 nonetheless, obtained by reducing minimum degree 3 on 8 vertices to the 3-regular case (a vertex of degree ≥5 gives 31>28 cherries; two degree-4 vertices give 30>28; exactly one degree-4 vertex makes the degree sum 25, odd, contradicting the handshake identity) and then a purely local argument that a 3-regular C₄-free graph on 8 vertices is impossible: every vertex lies in a unique triangle (else its three neighbours' punctured neighbourhoods pack 6 vertices into the remaining 4, or two triangles through a vertex force a C₄/higher degree), so the triangles would partition the 8 vertices into disjoint 3-sets — but 3 ∤ 8. The Lean proof builds this via `containsC4_of_two_common` (two common neighbours make a rim C₄), an explicit triangle-existence/uniqueness pair (`exists_triangle_of_three_regular`, `triangle_pair_unique`) on `SimpleGraph (Fin 8)`, and `containsC4_of_three_regular_eight`/`containsC4_of_eight_min_degree_three` assembling the degree-reduction and the triangle-partition contradiction. This breaks the 'needs ex(n;C₄) tables' barrier for the first even order past the counting threshold. All axiom-free.
sections.mathContext: 3-regular $C_4$-free on 8 vertices forces every vertex into a unique triangle (else a $C_4$ or excess degree), so the triangles partition $V$ into $\lvert V\rvert/3$ disjoint 3-sets — impossible since $3 \nmid 8$. Combined with the handshake-parity reduction from arbitrary $\delta \ge 3$ down to the 3-regular case, this pins $f(8)=3$ without any extremal-table ($\mathrm{ex}(8;C_4)=11$) input.

sections.title: Overturning the f(9) Blocker: the Pigeonhole C₄ Engine (axiom-free)
sections.summary: The remaining open exact value below the Petersen threshold is f(9); a prior session recorded the route as blocked pending ex(9;C₄)-table input. This section overturns that: `containsC4_of_degree_sum_subset`, `containsC4_of_card_add_two_le_degree_add_degree`, `card_inter_neighborFinset_le_one`, and `containsC4_of_four_set_min_two` build a pigeonhole engine — if two non-adjacent vertices' neighbourhoods are large enough relative to a small forbidden set, their common-neighbour count forces a rim C₄. `containsC4_of_nine_one_four`, `nine_degree_pinch`, and `containsC4_of_nine_three_fours` case-split a minimum-degree-3 graph on 9 vertices by how many vertices attain degree exactly 3 vs higher, closing every case via the pigeonhole engine. `containsC4_of_nine_min_degree_three` assembles the full case analysis, and `minDegreeForC4_nine`: f(9) = 3 — obtained without any ex(n;C₄) extremal-table input, overturning the recorded blocker. The exact-value table now reads f = 1,2,3,2,3,3,3,3,3 for n = 1,…,9; the next value, f(10) = 4, is the Petersen threshold. All axiom-free.
sections.mathContext: The pigeonhole engine: if $x,y$ are non-adjacent with combined neighbourhood large enough relative to $|V|$, their neighbourhoods overlap in $\ge 2$ vertices, giving two common neighbours and a rim $C_4$. Case-splitting the 9-vertex, minimum-degree-3 graph by how many vertices exceed degree 3 lets every branch meet this threshold, closing $f(9)=3$ without the extremal edge-count table $\mathrm{ex}(9;C_4)$ a prior session recorded as necessary.

sections.title: f(10) = 4: the Petersen Graph, Decide-Free at the Global Level (axiom-free)
sections.summary: The lower half f(10) ≥ 4 needs a C₄-free graph of minimum degree 3 on ten vertices — the Petersen graph, and by the Moore bound nothing smaller works. The route recorded as blocked ('kernel decide over the 10⁴ injective maps') is avoided entirely: `exists_two_common_of_containsC4` extracts any containsC4 witness to a pair of vertices with two distinct common neighbours, so `not_containsC4_of_forall_common_le_one` reduces C₄-freeness to the 10×10 common-neighbour matrix — a tiny kernel check. The graph itself is the explicit edge-list Petersen (`petersenEdges`, `petersen`): outer 5-cycle, inner pentagram, five spokes. `petersen_degree` (3-regular), `petersen_common_le_one` (the 10×10 kernel check), and `petersen_not_containsC4` establish the witness; `four_le_minDegreeForC4_ten` gives the lower half. `minDegreeForC4_ten`: f(10) = 4 exactly — upper half by plain counting (C(10,2)=45 < 60=10·C(4,2)). The exact table now reads f = 1,2,3,2,3,3,3,3,3,4 for n=1,…,10 — the first value exceeding 3, witnessing the √n growth. All axiom-free.
sections.mathContext: Common-neighbour extraction turns `containsC4`-freeness into a finite $10\times10$ matrix check (`petersen_common_le_one`, kernel `decide`), avoiding the blocked route of a $10^4$-embedding search. The Petersen graph is the unique $(3,5)$-Moore graph — 3-regular, girth 5, hence $C_4$-free — giving $f(10)\ge 4$; plain counting ($45<60$) gives $f(10)\le 4$, pinning $f(10)=4$ exactly, the first value where the threshold strictly exceeds 3.

conclusion.summary: We formalize Erdős Problem #85, which asks whether the minimum degree threshold f(n) for forcing a 4-cycle is eventually monotone. The asymptotic behavior f(n) ~ √n is well-understood, but the monotonicity question remains open.
conclusion.implications: This problem connects extremal graph theory to Ramsey theory through the relationship between f(n) and R(C₄, K_{1,n}). Understanding monotonicity would shed light on how the structure of extremal C₄-free graphs changes with the number of vertices.
openQuestions: Is f(n+1) ≥ f(n) for all large n?
Is f only 'almost monotone' (decreases by at most a constant)?
What is the exact relationship between f(n) and R(C₄, K_{1,n})?
Can we characterize extremal C₄-free graphs with high minimum degree?
